vignette:
The Weight of What He Carries

Marcus is a 27-year-old Filipino journalist who covers human rights stories for a regional online publication. He is thoughtful, articulate, and quick to deflect attention away from himself - a habit that served him well in his work for years, pointing the camera outward, always outward, until there was nothing left to look at but the wreckage inside.

For nearly two years, Marcus was in a relationship with a man he describes as "magnetic." They met at a press event. The relationship moved fast. Within four months they were living together, and within six, the first incident happened - a shove against a kitchen counter that left Marcus winded and confused. He told himself it was stress. His partner was under pressure. It wouldn't happen again. It happened again. Over the following year, the violence escalated: punches to the torso where bruises wouldn't show, hands around his throat during arguments, a ceramic mug thrown at his head that left a small scar above his right ear. Marcus stayed. He stayed because he loved him, because he was ashamed, because in his family and community the idea of a man being hurt by another man carried a particular silence around it - the kind that feels like suffocation.

He left fourteen months ago, after a night that ended with him sitting on the bathroom floor, door locked, blood from a split lip dripping onto the tiles, listening to his partner apologize through the wood. He packed a bag the next morning while his partner was at work and never went back.

Marcus is now in a new relationship with a woman he describes as kind and patient. He wants to be present for her. He finds he cannot always manage it. Some evenings, when she raises her voice even slightly - over something trivial, a parking dispute, a delayed dinner - Marcus goes somewhere else entirely. His body tightens, his vision narrows, and he is back on that bathroom floor. He has grabbed her wrist once, not in anger but in reflex, and the look on her face afterward stays with him like a photograph he cannot stop developing.

He does not sleep well. He wakes most nights between two and four in the morning with his heart slamming, unsure for a moment where he is or who is beside him. He checks the locks. He checks them again. At work, he sits with his back to the wall in every room he enters, something his colleagues have started to notice and joke about. He cannot write about domestic violence stories - and there are many in his beat - without his hands shaking over the keyboard. He has filed two incomplete drafts in the past three months and told his editor he's been unwell.

What troubles Marcus most is not the nightmares or the hypervigilance, though those exhaust him. It is the shame that has calcified around the whole experience. He grew up watching his father work long hours to provide, watching his mother hold the household together with quiet dignity. There was no language in that house for what happened to him. He finds himself wondering, still, whether he provoked it. Whether a different version of himself - stronger, smarter, less naive - would have left sooner, or never stayed at all. He has told almost no one. His parents believe he ended the relationship because of incompatibility. His closest friend knows only that it "got bad."

He sits in sessions with a kind of careful composure, his journalist's instinct for structure evident in the way he organizes his disclosures, presenting them almost as a story happening to someone else. But occasionally the composure slips - when he talks about the scar above his ear, when he mentions the bathroom floor - and something raw and unguarded moves across his face, and he looks, for just a moment, exactly his age.
